Chapter 1: Childhood in a Changing World — Traditions, Family, and Early Doubts
Picture this: before the world was cracked open by war, life in late Victorian and Edwardian England just moved to its own steady rhythm. There was a kind of comfort in that predictability—a sense that things would always be done the way they’d been done for generations. In one family’s home, every day was shaped by rituals and expectations. The kids grew up surrounded by all the markers of middle-class respectability, learning early that there were rules for everything—how you spoke, how you dressed, even how you thought about your place in the world.
At the center of this family stood the father—a man who believed deeply in discipline and the importance of family honor. The mother, always loving, was often caught up in the whirlwind of running a large household and handling all the social obligations that came with their status. The children were caught somewhere in between—torn between affection and formality. They learned quickly that emotions were best kept in check, and that questioning tradition was something you just didn’t do out loud.
School didn’t offer much of an escape. In fact, it felt like just more of the same. The classrooms were cold, the teachers even colder, and lessons were all about memorizing facts instead of feeding curiosity. For a boy growing up in that world, the pressure to fit in was enormous. Everything seemed to depend on how well you could mold yourself to expectations—not how much you actually understood, or cared. Vulnerability? Self-doubt? There just wasn’t room for that.
But, even in this tightly-wound world, cracks started to appear. This boy began to notice how the adults around him seemed weighed down by worries they almost never talked about. There were hushed conversations about money, about the future, about the world changing just outside their doors. All those old certainties? They didn’t feel so certain anymore. Even as he tried to keep up with what was expected of him, he felt a creeping unease—a suspicion that the world he was being prepared for might not even last.
Thank goodness for friends at school. In their company, there was finally a little room to breathe—a place for laughter, for a bit of mischief, and for honest conversations that just weren’t possible with adults. Still, even here, competition hovered in the background. Every test, every game, every single social interaction felt like a measure of your worth. And that fear of slipping up, of not measuring up? It was always there.
As adolescence rolled in, the boy found himself questioning the values he’d grown up with. He started to notice that the adults preaching duty and sacrifice weren’t exactly happy themselves. They seemed trapped—held hostage by the very traditions they insisted on keeping alive. It made him wonder: was there another way to live? One with a bit more honesty, a bit more kindness, a bit more freedom? But those kinds of thoughts were risky, so he kept them mostly to himself.
Beyond the family walls, the world was shifting, too. News of political unrest, incredible new inventions, even far-off wars, trickled in through newspapers and bits of overheard conversation on the street. That old feeling of security, once so strong, was starting to slip away. Most people tried their best to ignore all the changes, clinging tightly to the routines that gave life its meaning. But if you were really paying attention, you could sense a storm was brewing.
Looking back, it’s clear those seeds of doubt were planted early. The gap between what was taught and what was real just kept growing. The old rituals, once a source of comfort, started to feel empty. And so, the boy—like so many in his generation—found himself stuck between two worlds: one fading away, and another, not quite here yet, waiting just beyond the horizon.
